source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Main meta-analysis. Nudges move behaviour by a small to medium amount on average. The size depends on technique and domain. Authors flag moderate publication bias.
numbers: 455 effect sizes, 214 publications, N=2,149,683. d=0.45 (95% CI 0.39-0.52), t(340)=14.38. After outlier removal d=0.42. Leave-one-out d range 0.43-0.46. Raw d ranged -0.69 to 4.69. I2=99.67%, tau2=0.23. 95% prediction interval -0.48 to 1.39, so about 15% of interventions are likely to backfire.
limits: A later correction gives d=0.43 for the corrected data. Heterogeneity is almost total, so the mean says little about any one nudge. Many effects come from lab or online behaviour, not only field.
agent_relevance: G7: the average hides a huge spread. Any scaffold element borrowed from nudge ideas needs its own measurement, not trust in the mean.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) moderator results (decision structure vs information vs assistance; domains)
finding: Structure nudges (defaults, effort, option range, consequences) beat information nudges and assistance nudges (reminders, commitment). Food is the strongest domain, finance the weakest.
numbers: Structure vs information b=0.17 (95% CI 0.03-0.31, p=0.02). Structure vs assistance b=0.24 (0.11-0.36, p<0.001). Information vs assistance b=-0.07 (ns). Category means d=0.31 to 0.55. Nine techniques all positive, d=0.30-0.62. Domains d=0.25 (finance, CI 0.12-0.37) to 0.72 (food, CI 0.49-0.95). Moderators barely cut heterogeneity: I2 from 99.67% to 99.57% (category) and 99.58% (domain).
limits: Unadjusted for publication bias. After adjustment, information and assistance shrink to about zero (see b04).
agent_relevance: Changing the structure of the choice (what is on the menu, what is the default) is worth more than adding information. For the agent: restructure the option set before adding advice text.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) publication bias and sensitivity analysis (same paper)
finding: The funnel plot is lopsided: small studies report big positive effects. The authors' own sensitivity analysis shrinks the effect a lot if bias is severe.
numbers: Egger's test b=2.28 (95% CI 1.31-3.25), t(339)=4.61, p<0.001. Moderate one-tailed bias: d falls 26.79% from 0.42 to 0.31. Severe one-tailed bias: d=0.03 (the reply letter quotes d=0.08).
quote: attenuated the overall effect size of choice architecture interventions by 26.79%
limits: The authors kept the conclusion unchanged and then mostly ignored bias in the moderator analyses. Critics called the bias the real headline.
agent_relevance: Small positive demos of a scaffold trick are exactly the case G7 warns about. Require equal-token comparison and larger N.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA, mixing selection models and PET-PEESE) on the corrected Mertens data. The overall effect drops to about zero. Information and assistance nudges show evidence for no effect. Structure nudges are undecided.
numbers: Combined: random effects d=0.43 [0.38,0.48] vs RoBMA 0.04 [0.00,0.14], BF01=0.95. Using only the most precise estimate per study: 0.11 [0.00,0.24], BF01=0.31. Information 0.25 to 0.00 (BF01=33.84). Structure 0.58 to 0.12 [0.00,0.43] (BF01=1.12; precise 0.23, BF01=0.33). Assistance 0.22 to 0.01 (BF01=9.05). Food 0.66 to 0.02 (BF01=5.16; precise 0.27, BF01=0.55). Finance 0.23 to 0.00 (BF01=41.23). Strong evidence of publication bias in all subdomains (BFpb>10) except food on precise estimates (2.49).
quote: no evidence remains that nudges are effective as tools for behaviour change
limits: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: structure and food stay undecided. The three-level model could not be bias-corrected, so clustering was ignored or one estimate per study kept. Letter format, short.
agent_relevance: After correction, the one nudge class that plausibly survives is structure. This matches the idea that changing the option set beats added exhortation. Still unproven.

source: Maier et al. (2022) heterogeneity point (same letter)
finding: Even with a zero average, some nudges can work: there is evidence of heterogeneity in every subgroup except finance.
numbers: Heterogeneity supported in all intervention categories and domains apart from finance. They call Mertens' Egger coefficient b=2.10 'severe' by the Doucouliagos-Stanley rule of thumb.
limits: Heterogeneity may itself come from varying bias.
agent_relevance: Do not average across tasks. Test each scaffold element per task type and keep only the ones that win.

source: Szaszi, Higney, Charlton, Gelman, Ziano, Aczel, Goldstein, Yeager, Tipton (2022) No reason to expect large and consistent effects of nudge interventions
finding: Reanalysis of the same database with three bias-correction methods gives near-zero means and huge spread. Argues for studying when nudges work, not averages. Defaults are the main exception.
numbers: Andrews-Kasy d=-0.01 (SE 0.02). WAAP d=0.07 (SE 0.03). Trim-and-fill d=0.08 (SE 0.03). Mertens' own adjusted range d=0.08 (severe) to 0.31 (moderate). Under severe bias, 95% of true effects would lie within +/-1.00 of 0.08.
quote: we see no reason to expect large and consistent effects when designing nudge experiments
limits: Trim-and-fill can over-correct when heterogeneity is high. The methods are not independent of each other.
agent_relevance: Plan for 'effect varies by context' as the default assumption. Log which task types each element helps.

source: Bakdash and Marusich (2022) Left-truncated effects and overestimated meta-analytic means
finding: Plots of effect distributions show a left cliff at zero, so negative results are missing. Pooled means are overestimates: 63% of effects sit below the overall mean.
numbers: Share of effects below domain mean (50% would be representative): environment 55.26%, finance 55.56%, food 60.36%, health 72.62%, other 49.32%, prosocial 67.39%, overall 62.64%. Domain means d: environment 0.43, finance 0.24, food 0.65, health 0.34, other 0.31, prosocial 0.41. Egger p<0.001 in most domains, p=0.01 in finance and food.
limits: Descriptive. No corrected pooled estimate. 12 prosocial effects with |d|<0.04 were dropped for estimation problems.
agent_relevance: Skewed, truncated distributions mean the typical result of a prompt trick is worse than the headline. Report medians and failures.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) Reply to Maier, Szaszi, and Bakdash and Marusich
finding: The original authors concede that publication bias and heterogeneity are real problems. They say the paper was not meant as the final word and call for better-powered and preregistered studies.
numbers: Restates d=0.43 uncorrected, Egger b=2.10 [1.31,2.89], t(332)=5.22. Adjusted d=0.31 (moderate bias) and 0.08 (severe). Agrees the letters' methods give smaller or null effects.
limits: A reply, not new data. They did not rerun RoBMA.
agent_relevance: Both sides agree the evidence base is biased and heterogeneous. Treat nudge-derived scaffold ideas as hypotheses.

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units (Econometrica)
finding: All trials of two big US nudge units (126 RCTs, 23 million people) show effects about one sixth of those in academic journals. Selective publication plus low power explain about 70% of the gap.
numbers: 126 RCTs, 23 million individuals. Academic journals sample: 8.7 percentage point take-up effect (33.4% over control). Nudge units: 1.4 percentage points (8.0%). Publication bias and low power explain about 70% of the gap; topic and behavioural channel explain most of the rest.
quote: selective publication in the Academic Journals sample, exacerbated by low statistical power, explains about 70 percent
limits: Abstract read (Crossref record), not the full paper. Nudge-unit tests are mostly mail and message nudges on take-up; defaults and structure changes are rarer.
agent_relevance: Strong G7 case: effect shrinks about 6x from showcase to deployment. Expect the same when a scaffold moves from tuned demos to the full benchmark.

source: Milkman et al. (2021) Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science (Nature)
finding: 54 interventions to raise gym visits were tested together on 61,293 members. Many helped, but little, and carry-over was rare. Experts could not predict the winners.
numbers: N=61,293, 54 interventions, 30 scientists, 15 universities. 45% significantly raised weekly gym visits, by 9% to 27%. Only 8% still significant after the 4-week programme. Top intervention: microrewards for returning after a missed workout. Forecasts by judges failed to predict which would win.
limits: Abstract read (Europe PMC record). One setting (US fitness chain), 4 weeks. Same-population testing removes between-study publication bias by design.
agent_relevance: A megastudy is the model for testing scaffold elements: many variants, same items, same budget, pre-registered, then rank. Also: do not trust our own forecast of which element wins.

source: Milkman et al. (2022) A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies (PNAS)
finding: 22 text reminders for flu shots. All beat control, but gains were small. The best message said a vaccine was 'waiting for you' and was sent twice. Forecasters missed the winner.
numbers: N=689,693 Walmart pharmacy customers, 22 messages. Average gain 2.0 percentage points (6.8%) over a business-as-usual control.
limits: Abstract read only (Crossref). One retailer, one flu season.
agent_relevance: Wording differences inside a good nudge family matter less than having the nudge at all; heavy wording tuning is low value.

source: Milkman et al. (2024) Megastudy shows that reminders boost vaccination but adding free rides does not (Nature)
finding: Eight interventions for COVID booster uptake. Free rides, which experts and laypeople forecast to work, added nothing beyond text reminders. Reminders helped.
numbers: Reminders raised 30-day booster uptake by 21% (1.05 percentage points) on average and flu shots by 8% (0.34 points). Best 'make a plan' message +23.65% (1.20 points). Infection-rate message +21.71% (1.11). Pharmacy-team message +21.57% (1.10; adjusted p=0.126 vs baseline). Gap between best and worst intervention only 0.26 points. Cells about 492,573 patients each; free-ride arm 50,000.
limits: US only, one pharmacy chain. The free-ride arm was smaller than the other cells.
agent_relevance: Intuitively appealing add-ons can add nothing. Directly supports ablation: remove each scaffold step and see whether the score moves.

source: Field testing the transferability of behavioural science knowledge on promoting vaccinations (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024)
finding: Three pre-registered RCTs. Reminders and psychological-ownership wording replicated earlier field results. Ideas that scored well in intention surveys or expert forecasts gave no gain over a simple reminder.
numbers: 3 RCTs, N=314,824 UCLA Health patients in the analysis. Ownership language and reminders raised booster uptake. Bundling flu and COVID shots and misconception messages: no detectable benefit over a simple reminder. Companion online experiments: 1,774 and 989 participants (outcome: perceived persuasiveness).
limits: One health system. I did not extract the per-arm effect sizes from the paper body.
agent_relevance: Hypothetical and intention-based tests overpredict field results. For the agent: judge a scaffold step by end-task accuracy, not by whether the reasoning trace looks good.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: meta-analysis of default effects
finding: Defaults are the strongest nudge in this literature but vary. Some studies find no effect and two find negative effects. They work better when they signal endorsement or the status quo.
numbers: 58 studies, pooled n=73,675. d=0.68 (95% CI 0.53-0.83). Consumer domain stronger, environmental weaker. Defaults stronger when seen as endorsed by the choice architect or as the status quo.
limits: Abstract read only. I do not know whether it was corrected for publication bias. Szaszi et al. singled defaults out as an exception.
agent_relevance: The default is the best-supported nudge. For an agent, the analogue is the starting hypothesis or first option shown, which anchors what follows (see b19, b23).

source: Beshears and Kosowsky (2020) Nudging: Progress to date and future directions (OBHDP)
finding: Review of 174 articles. Nudges that automate part of the decision are bigger than the others. Calls for long-run and spillover measurement.
numbers: 174 articles. Automating nudges have an average Cohen's d 0.193 larger than other nudges.
limits: Abstract read only. Not bias-corrected.
agent_relevance: Automation (do the step for the user) beats exhortation (tell the user to do the step). In scaffold terms: code that enforces a check beats a prompt that asks for one.

source: Benartzi et al. (2017) Should Governments Invest More in Nudging? (Psychological Science)
finding: Impact per dollar of nudges often compares well with classical tools such as tax incentives, even when absolute effects are small.
numbers: Ratios of impact to cost computed for nudges and traditional policy tools; nudges often favourable. No single pooled figure extracted.
limits: Abstract read only. Cost-effectiveness depends on the small effect surviving at scale, which DellaVigna and Linos question.
agent_relevance: Cost matters. Cheap, small-gain scaffold steps can be worth keeping, but only if the token cost is counted (G7).

source: Bryan, Tipton, Yeager (2021) Behavioural science is unlikely to change the world without a heterogeneity revolution (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Replication failures are expected when effects vary by setting. Recommends sampling and moderation designs that measure how effects vary, plus shared research infrastructure.
numbers: Conceptual paper. No pooled estimate. Argues most treatment effects are heterogeneous.
limits: Abstract read only. A framing argument, not a test.
agent_relevance: Explains why a scaffold tuned on ARC may fail on another benchmark. Evaluate on varied item sets and report the spread.

source: Horton (2023) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
finding: LLMs can replicate classic behavioural economics experiments qualitatively, including status quo bias from Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988). Some models show strong status quo bias, others little.
numbers: Status quo replication on GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Claude 3.7 and DeepSeek, 6,999 choices pooled. The status quo indicator is significant for every model, smallest for GPT-4o. Options farther from the status quo are less likely to be chosen.
limits: I read the abstract and the status quo section. The table text was garbled in extraction, so per-model coefficients were not recorded. Qualitative replication, not matched effect sizes.
agent_relevance: A status quo or default framed in a prompt pulls model choices. The order and framing of a first hypothesis matter.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 shows anchoring, the conjunction fallacy, framing and endowment effects, like humans on the same prompts.
numbers: Anchoring: low-anchor mean 20.83 (CI 13.92-27.74) vs human 22.5; high-anchor 105.97 (CI 87.40-124.54) vs human 80.50. ChatGPT low vs high t(58)=8.78, p<0.0001; humans t(58)=5.55. ChatGPT vs human at high anchor p=0.06. Conjunction: ChatGPT chose the conjunction 18 of 20 times. Framing: positive-frame efficacy rating 5.2 vs negative 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<0.001.
limits: GPT-3.5 only, small N, old model. Hagendorff et al. report that such biases fade in GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Framing and anchors in the prompt move answers. The schema should counterbalance option order and keep question wording neutral.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs and disappeared in GPT-4
finding: GPT-3 behaves like fast human intuition on the Cognitive Reflection Test and semantic illusions. ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid the errors and act hyperrationally.
numbers: Abstract only: CRT and semantic illusions; GPT-3 makes human-like errors, GPT-4 and ChatGPT do not. No numbers extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Task-specific: stronger models still show other biases (b21, b23).
agent_relevance: Bias susceptibility depends on model generation. Re-measure biases on the model the agent actually uses.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief biases. Pretrained models show little.
numbers: In one table fragment: decoy-expensive bias score 0.00 (base) vs 0.38* (instruction-tuned); certainty 0.20* vs 0.15*. Models: GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families, Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
limits: Numbers from one table fragment. Family patterns vary, and in a larger Flan-T5 variant decoy bias moved the other way. Stronger models are not uniformly less biased.
agent_relevance: Tuning for helpfulness can make models more nudgeable. What options and decoys appear in the prompt matters more for tuned models.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: 13,465 prompts test prompt-induced, sequential and inherent biases in LLM admissions decisions. Prompt framing changes decisions. Self-help debiasing works best. Few-shot mitigation can break instruction following.
numbers: GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject framing than under the admit framing. Llama-2 7B classifies 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Models prefer early options (primacy). Self-help debiasing: GPT-4 group-attribution bias elements to 0% and framing to 2.7%; Llama-2 13B framing 0%, 7B 1.4%; GPT-3.5 cut group attribution only 8.9% and left framing and status quo at 17.2% and 8.5%. Llama models change 40-52% of decisions when asked to debias their own anchored choices. Few-shot and counterfactual mitigation can drive admission rates to 0 or 1.
limits: Synthetic admissions scenario, not a nudge study as such. Capacity-dependent: low-capacity models cannot self-debias.
agent_relevance: A neutral rewrite step (the model strips bias-inducing wording from its own prompt) works for strong models only. Use it only if tested on the actual model. Few-shot examples can backfire.

source: Allouah, Besbes, Figueroa, Kanoria, Kumar (2025) What Is Your AI Agent Buying? Evaluation, biases, model dependence (ACES)
finding: Randomised trials on shopping agents show strong position effects, badge effects (endorsement up, sponsored down), and sensitivities that differ by model and version. Telling the agent to ignore position does not fix it.
numbers: Conditional logit, top-row coefficient: 1.224 (Claude Sonnet 4), 1.045 (GPT-4.1), 0.344 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), all p<0.001. Moving a product from 4.5% share at bottom right to the top row gives a 5-fold rise for Claude Sonnet 4. An 'Overall Pick' tag lifts a 10% baseline to 24.3%, 19.9% and 42.6%. A 'Sponsored' tag lowers it to 8.9%, 8.0% and 7.9%. Scarcity tag: no clear effect. GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.1 have nearly opposite position biases. Seller-side description tweaks gained +3.66 to +14.89 percentage points of share in 5 of 6 models. The prompt 'ignore position' did not significantly cut position effects. Effects persist in a text-only API setting.
limits: Mock shopping site, eight products per page, 2025 models. Market-share gains depend on the seller agent used.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that LLM agents are nudged by layout, order and endorsement badges, and that prompt warnings do not remove it. Fix by shuffling and counterbalancing in code, then measure (G7).

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT (PNAS)
finding: GPT's budget choices are largely consistent with utility maximisation, more than humans, but sensitive to the wording of the choice context.
numbers: Four domains: risk, time, social, food. Rationality scores (revealed preference) higher than human subjects in a parallel experiment and in the literature. Robust to randomness and demographic settings; sensitive to language frames.
limits: Abstract read only. No numbers extracted. Consistency with utility is not the same as a correct decision.
agent_relevance: LLMs can be consistent yet frame-dependent. Frame sensitivity is the risk to test for.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Codex errs predictably with prompt framing, drifts toward anchors, and copies frequent training patterns.
numbers: Code-generation case study. Framing, anchoring and frequency biases demonstrated. No pooled number extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Codex is an old model.
agent_relevance: Use known human biases as a checklist to design tests of the agent's failure modes.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 does well on many vignette decision tasks and bandits, but small rewordings throw it off and it fails a causal reasoning task.
numbers: Battery of canonical experiments. Outperforms humans in a multi-armed bandit. Shows no directed exploration. Fails the causal task.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Small wording perturbations flip answers. Supports consistency checks across paraphrases.

source: Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo, Iwasawa (2022) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
finding: A one-line nudge, 'Let's think step by step', lifts accuracy a lot on older models. It is the best-known nudge in LLM work.
numbers: text-davinci-002: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%. GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%.
limits: Large effect on weak 2022 models. Later models reason by default, so the gain probably shrinks; measure again on current models. Not a choice-architecture study.
agent_relevance: Prompt nudges can work, but the gain depends on the model. Re-measure at equal tokens, because step-by-step costs more tokens (G7).

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five assistants lean toward the user's stated view. Humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones.
numbers: Five state-of-the-art assistants across four free-form tasks all show sycophancy. Optimising against preference models sometimes trades truth for it.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The user's wording is itself a nudge. The agent should not treat hints about the expected answer as evidence.

source: Fei et al. (2024) Nudging: Inference-time Alignment of LLMs via Guided Decoding
finding: Engineering use of the word: a small aligned model steps in at uncertain tokens to guide a base model. It matches or beats large aligned models without training.
numbers: A base model nudged by a 7x-14x smaller aligned model reaches zero-shot performance comparable to large aligned models. Gemma-2-27b nudged with Llama-2-7b-chat beats Llama-2-70b-chat on several tasks.
limits: Same name, different thing: not a behavioural nudge. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A cheap small-model guide at high-uncertainty points is a tested pattern for training-free steering.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models, like humans, show content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: LMs reason better when content matches real-world belief, like humans, so topic and wording change logic performance.
numbers: Abstract: human-like content effects across logical reasoning tasks. No numbers extracted.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on neutral and belief-congruent versions of the same problem.

source: Jia et al. (2024) Decision-Making Behavior Evaluation Framework for LLMs under Uncertain Context
finding: A framework measures risk preference, probability weighting and loss aversion in LLMs.
numbers: Abstract only. No figures extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Results unverified by me.
agent_relevance: A possible battery to check whether the agent's risk handling is distorted.
